passage: Snow was piling against the window of the Toronto flat when Tariq came back from his shift. "Oh, you're home," Amira said. "Thought you might stay out with your new favourite coworker." She laughed, but it came out thin. Tariq frowned and put the groceries down. Later she took her plate to the bedroom and shut the door, waiting to see if he would knock. He did, after twenty minutes, looking tired. While he showered, his phone lit up on the bed. Her hand hovered. She picked it up, read nothing but a delivery message, and felt no better at all. When he came out, he saw the phone in a different spot. He said nothing, and the silence sat between them all evening.

qa.q: Where did Tariq's phone light up?
qa.a: His phone lit up on the bed while he showered.

qa.q: Why did Amira shut the bedroom door with her plate?
qa.a: She wanted to test whether Tariq would come after her, hoping it would prove he still cared.

qa.q: What turning point is available for Amira now?
qa.a: Instead of more tests, she could tell Tariq plainly that she has been feeling insecure, because the checks are not calming her and are starting to hurt him.

qa.q: How is Tariq likely experiencing these tests?
qa.a: He seems worn out and uneasy; the joke, the closed door and the moved phone may make him feel watched and distrusted. 😔

grounding: It shows a young woman using half-joking jabs, withdrawal to see if he follows, and a phone check that brings no reassurance and strains both people.

passage: The hostel common room was empty except for Himani and Parth, sharing a packet of chips before the library closed. "So, is your lab partner coming to the fest too?" she asked, grinning a little too wide. "Maybe you two can present together, you're such a team." Parth laughed awkwardly. "Himani, she's just my lab partner." "Relax, I'm joking." Her friend Pallavi, passing with a laundry bucket, caught Himani's eye and raised an eyebrow. Later Himani didn't answer Parth's goodnight text, just to see if he'd call. He called twice, then stopped. Next morning he looked like he hadn't slept. "Are we okay?" he asked, and she heard herself say, "You tell me."

qa.q: Where were Himani and Parth sharing chips?
qa.a: They were in the hostel common room.

qa.q: What might Himani want when she ignores Parth's goodnight text?
qa.a: She seems to want proof that he cares enough to chase her, because she is afraid of losing him to his lab partner.

qa.q: What could turn things around for Himani at this stage?
qa.a: She could drop the half jokes and the silence and tell Parth honestly that she feels insecure, so he is not left guessing.

qa.q: What is it like for Parth right now?
qa.a: He looks sleepless and unsure, asking "Are we okay?" because the jokes and silence leave him worried without knowing why.

grounding: It illustrates provoking with teasing remarks and pulling away to test the partner, which wears both of them down.

passage:
The bus from Jaipur to Ajmer was two hours late, the waiting room was hot, and Rukmini had been testing Jagdish all afternoon.

"You'd probably rather be travelling with Neha from your office," she said, laughing, as if it were a joke.

Jagdish smiled uncertainly. "Why would I?"

Later she moved to a bench across the room and scrolled on her phone, watching from the corner of her eye to see whether he'd follow. He didn't. He thought she wanted space. That, too, went into her list.

When he went to buy water, he left his phone on the seat. She picked it up and read his last few messages. Nothing. Work, his mother, a cricket score.

She put it back, heart pounding, and felt no better. Just ashamed, and still afraid.

When Jagdish came back, he looked tired. "Rukmini, are we okay? You've been... different all day."

qa.q: Why were they stuck in the waiting room?
qa.a: The bus from Jaipur to Ajmer was two hours late.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel after reading Jagdish's messages and finding nothing?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and still afraid; the test gave no reassurance.

qa.q: What went wrong with Rukmini's tests, and what could she do instead?
qa.a: Her half-joking remarks, pulling away and checking his phone wore them both down without easing her fear; she could tell Jagdish honestly that she feels insecure.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish to be tested all afternoon?
qa.a: He feels confused and tired, sensing something is wrong without knowing what, which could slowly push him away.

grounding: On a delayed journey Rukmini tests Jagdish with half-jokes, pulling away and checking his phone, which brings no reassurance and wears them both down.

passage:
Parveen had started making little jokes. "Oh, you're texting Sana again? Should I leave you two alone?" Kamal laughed the first few times. By the second month he didn't.

In their shared Mumbai flat, she tested him in other ways. She'd go quiet for a whole evening to see if he would notice and chase. He noticed. He asked. She said, "Nothing." He stopped asking after a while.

One night, while he showered, she read his chats with Sana, his colleague. Presentations. Deadlines. One joke about their boss. Nothing else.

She felt a rush of relief. Then, an hour later, the fear crept back: maybe they deleted things.

Kamal came out of the bathroom and saw his phone on her side of the bed. He didn't say anything. But he looked at her in a way he never had before, tired and a little distant.

The thing she feared most was starting to happen, and she had helped it along.

qa.q: Who is Sana?
qa.a: Kamal's colleague.

qa.q: What happened to Parveen's relief after reading the chats?
qa.a: It faded within an hour, and fear crept back that they had deleted things, showing tests don't reassure her.

qa.q: What could turn this around at this stage?
qa.a: Parveen could stop testing and tell Kamal honestly that she feels insecure, instead of joking, pulling away and checking.

qa.q: How does Kamal seem to feel when he sees his phone on her side of the bed?
qa.a: He seems hurt and tired, and more distant, worn down by the constant tests.

grounding: Parveen tests Kamal with half-joking remarks, pulling away and checking his phone, which brings no lasting reassurance and starts to make her fear real.

passage:
"Pradeep, who's Shruti?"

"From my study group. Why?"

"No reason. She's pretty. You must like the study group a lot." Elizabeth laughed.

"Is that a joke?"

"Obviously it's a joke."

"It didn't sound like one."

"Relax. Anyway, I'm not coming to the café tonight."

"Why not?"

"Just not feeling it."

"Okay. I'll miss you."

"Will you? Or will Shruti be there?"

"Elizabeth. What's going on?"

"...Can I see your phone?"

"Seriously?"

"If there's nothing, why not?"

"Fine. Here. Take it."

"...There's nothing."

"I told you."

"I know. Sorry. I don't feel better, though."

"That's what worries me. You keep checking and it never helps. I'm getting tired, Elizabeth."

qa.q: Who is Shruti, according to Pradeep?
qa.a: Someone from the study group.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel after checking the phone and finding nothing?
qa.a: Elizabeth still doesn't feel better; the fear stays, and Elizabeth feels sorry but not reassured.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth say instead of testing?
qa.a: Elizabeth could tell Pradeep plainly about feeling insecure and ask for reassurance, rather than joking, pulling away or checking Pradeep's phone.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep to be tested like this?
qa.a: Pradeep feels confused and increasingly tired, worried that the checking never helps.

grounding: In dialogue Elizabeth half-jokes about Pradeep's classmate, pulls away and checks Pradeep's phone, which brings no reassurance and wears Pradeep down.

passage: Looking back at last spring, I can see how, as Adil's girlfriend, I tested him like a science experiment, except I never learned anything. I'd say, half joking, "Go on, have fun with your gang, I'm sure everyone will be thrilled you're single for the night." Then I'd watch his face. Some days I went cold on purpose and left his messages unanswered, just to see if he'd chase me. He usually did, for a while. Once, while he was in the shower, I opened his phone and scrolled through his chats. Nothing. And still I felt worse, not better, like a thief. My friend Rashmi said, "Hafsa, you're asking him to pass a test he doesn't know he's taking." She was right. Adil got quieter and more tired, and by May he said, "I feel like I'm always on trial." That sentence frightened me more than any imagined rival ever had.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do while Adil was in the shower?
qa.a: She opened his phone and scrolled through his chats.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after checking Adil's phone and finding nothing?
qa.a: She felt worse, not relieved, and guilty like a thief, because the test gave her no real reassurance.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done instead of setting tests?
qa.a: She could have told Adil plainly that she felt insecure and asked for reassurance, instead of provoking him to prove himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Adil to be tested without knowing it?
qa.a: Adil grew quiet and tired and felt he was always on trial, which wore down the closeness Hafsa was trying to protect.

grounding: Shows a young woman testing her partner with half-joking remarks, pulling away and checking his phone, and how it wears them both down.
